patterns_data.top_pattern: GA acute hospital admissions are driving the largest spend increase
patterns_data.what_is_impacting: GA PPO Local acute hospital spend
patterns_data.pattern_details: GA PPO Local acute hospital spend rose primarily because inpatient claim volume increased sharply. There is also a smaller unit-cost increase on a high-cost medical inpatient pocket, but the main story is more hospital activity, not just higher prices. This is the clearest operational utilization issue in the analysis.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: This is the single largest clearly actionable medical cost trend and points to immediate utilization management leverage in GA acute hospitals.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Pull GA PPO Local acute hospital claims to identify the facilities and service lines behind the claim growth, then apply admission management and reimbursement review to the highest-growth hospitals.
evidence_summary: GA acute hospital spend increased about $2.8M in PPO Local.
The increase was driven by about 1,970 more claims in GA acute hospitals.
A smaller acute hospital unit-cost pocket added about $42K even with 1 fewer claim, with paid per admit up about $23.5K.

patterns_data.top_pattern: GA not-mapped inpatient claims are masking a major cost driver
patterns_data.what_is_impacting: GA PPO Local inpatient and facility classification
key_driver_codes: Other Disorders of Nervous System without CC/MCC
patterns_data.pattern_details: A large share of GA PPO Local spend is sitting in not-mapped inpatient buckets, both within acute hospitals and under unmapped facility classification. Claim counts and paid per case both increased, so the organization cannot yet tell how much is true utilization, how much is pricing, and how much is coding or classification movement. This should be treated as a gating validation issue before broad policy or contracting action.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: Without fixing the not-mapped buckets first, authorization, reimbursement, and provider actions risk targeting the wrong root cause.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Validate GA facility and DRG mapping for the not-mapped claims first, then rerun the inpatient review to separate true utilization growth from contract or payment leakage.
patterns_data.validation_reason: The dominant drivers are not-mapped DRG and not-mapped facility categories with material dollar impact and rising claim counts.
evidence_summary: GA acute hospital not-mapped DRG spend increased about $2.7M on roughly 2,001 more claims, with paid per admit up about $591.
GA not-mapped facility spend increased about $1.8M on roughly 2,239 more claims, with paid per admit up about $439.
Within the not-mapped facility bucket, not-mapped DRG added about $949K on roughly 2,189 more claims.

patterns_data.what_is_impacting: CA PPO Local acute hospital and rehab spend
key_driver_codes: Degenerative Nervous System Disorders without MCC
patterns_data.pattern_details: CA shows a large not-mapped hospital pattern, but unlike GA, the stronger signal is payment pressure rather than pure broad-based volume growth. One not-mapped facility bucket grew with claims, while an acute hospital not-mapped bucket rose even as claims declined, indicating higher paid per case. A smaller rehab unit-cost increase suggests some spillover beyond acute hospitals.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: CA needs validation first, but the remaining signal points to real reimbursement pressure if the mapping issue does not fully explain the increase.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Validate CA facility and DRG classification for the not-mapped claims, then review hospital payment logic and contracted rates for the acute hospital subset with higher paid per admit.
patterns_data.validation_reason: The largest CA drivers are concentrated in not-mapped categories, which could distort both utilization and unit-cost interpretation.
evidence_summary: CA not-mapped facility spend increased about $1.4M on roughly 3,419 more claims.
CA acute hospital not-mapped DRG spend increased about $1.1M even with about 201 fewer claims, with paid per admit up about $368.
CA Physical Rehab added about $43K with flat claim volume, indicating localized unit-cost pressure.

patterns_data.top_pattern: GA spend is spreading into SNF, ASC, rehab, and critical access sites
patterns_data.what_is_impacting: GA PPO Local non-acute and alternative facility spend
patterns_data.pattern_details: The GA cost trend is not limited to acute hospitals. Spend also increased across SNF, ambulatory surgery center, rehab, and critical access settings, with both more claims and higher paid per case in the largest pockets. This suggests a broader site-of-care and discharge-routing issue in GA PPO Local.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: When growth spreads across multiple facility types, authorization, discharge planning, and network pricing need to be addressed together rather than in isolated silos.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Run a GA site-of-care review across SNF, ASC, rehab, and critical access claims to confirm authorization criteria, discharge routing, and contracted rates at the fastest-growing facilities.
evidence_summary: GA SNF - FREE STANDING spend increased about $987K on roughly 153 more claims, with paid per admit up about $3.4K.
GA ambulatory surgery center spend increased about $517K on roughly 504 more claims.
GA Physical Rehab added about $86K across 3 claims, with paid per admit up about $28.6K.
GA Critical Access added about $36K, but on very low volume.

patterns_data.top_pattern: Low-volume provider pockets are creating acute hospital cost leakage
patterns_data.what_is_impacting: PPO Local acute hospital provider mix in CT / IN / MO / NY / VA
patterns_data.pattern_details: A small but recurring provider-mix pattern is emerging in acute hospitals across CT / IN / MO / NY / VA. Volumes are low, but the cases are concentrated in a few providers with much higher paid per case, which is more consistent with provider mix or episodic payment terms than with broad market demand. This should be handled as a targeted network economics review, not a marketwide utilization issue.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: Small provider pockets can become recurring leakage if they sit outside normal steerage, pricing, or case-rate controls.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Audit claims tied to HOSPITAL FOR SPECIAL SURGERY and WVU MEDICINE PRINCETON COMMUNITY HOSPITAL in the listed states for steerage patterns, single-case pricing, and contracted payment terms.
patterns_data.validation_reason: Most of the signal comes from low-volume provider pockets, so provider-level validation is needed before scaling action.
evidence_summary: The CT / IN / MO / NY / VA acute hospital pattern added about $265K overall.
A MO acute hospital pocket contributed about $116K on roughly 51 more claims.
HOSPITAL FOR SPECIAL SURGERY added about $55K in NY, $25K in CT, and $23K in IN.
WVU MEDICINE PRINCETON COMMUNITY HOSPITAL added about $46K in VA on 3 claims, with paid per admit up about $5.7K.

patterns_data.top_pattern: Rare inpatient and neuro cases are producing high-cost outliers
patterns_data.what_is_impacting: Rare IP Med/Surg and NF cases in CA / GA / NY / UNATTRIBUTED
key_driver_codes: Degenerative Nervous System Disorders without MCC
Other Disorders of Nervous System without CC/MCC
patterns_data.pattern_details: A set of rare inpatient and NF cases is creating meaningful spend through a small number of very expensive neurologic and medical admissions. These are not broad utilization trends; they are low-frequency, high-cost outliers, and several also carry missing or blank procedure information. The right response is combined clinical validation and case management, not broad utilization restriction.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: Rare high-cost cases can distort trend reading and require different action than routine inpatient growth.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Send these IP Med/Surg and NF cases to clinical and data-quality review to confirm true catastrophic complexity versus miscoding or missing procedures, then case-manage any repeat episodes.
patterns_data.validation_reason: The pattern is driven by low-volume high-cost cases with repeated unmapped or blank procedure fields.
evidence_summary: CA / NY / UNATTRIBUTED IP Med/Surg outliers added about $256K, including single cases of about $75.5K and $60.4K.
CA NF outliers added about $177K, led by G20C and I69354 cases of about $59.6K and $58.7K.
GA IP Med/Surg outliers added about $106K, led by R5381 and G959 cases.
GA NF outliers added about $45K on a handful of low-volume cases.

patterns_data.what_is_impacting: Outpatient specialty services in NY / UNATTRIBUTED / VA / GA
patterns_data.pattern_details: Several outpatient specialty claims are appearing in not-mapped surgery, oncology, and drug-management categories and are concentrated in a few providers. Volumes are small, so this looks less like broad demand growth and more like provider mix, specialty authorization, or coding classification movement. Validation should happen before expanding policy edits or provider actions.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: Outpatient specialty leakage can escalate quickly when specialty drugs or surgery claims bypass clean classification and provider-specific controls.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Validate outpatient specialty coding for the not-mapped surgery and drug episodes, then review provider-specific authorization edits and claim handling for HOSPITAL FOR SPECIAL SURGERY, WVU MEDICINE PRINCETON COMMUNITY HOSPITAL, and INNOVATIVE SUPPLY GROUP.
patterns_data.validation_reason: The pattern is concentrated in not-mapped outpatient categories, low-volume specialty claims, and a small set of providers.
